title: How to Check Your Credit Report for Errors
excerpt: An error on your credit report can be easy to miss. Learn what to check, what to save, and how to ask for a correction.

paragraphs: Your credit report tells a story about your accounts and payments. Before you focus on your score, make sure that story is right. A careful review can help you spot mistakes or signs that someone used your name to open an account.

sections.heading: Start with your free reports
paragraphs: You can get free weekly reports from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion through [AnnualCreditReport.com](https://www.annualcreditreport.com/index.action). Check all three. The FTC confirms that this free weekly program is available. You do not need to buy a credit repair service to get these reports. [See the FTC’s guide to free credit reports](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/free-credit-reports).

sections.heading: Check one section at a time
paragraphs: Look at your name, address, accounts, and payment history. Watch for:

- An account that is not yours.
- A payment marked late when you paid on time.
- A wrong balance or credit limit.
- An account shown as open after it was closed.
- The same debt listed more than once.

Compare anything that looks wrong with your own records. [The CFPB lists common report errors here](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-are-common-credit-report-errors-that-i-should-look-for-on-my-credit-report-en-313/).

sections.heading: Explain the error and keep proof
paragraphs: Dispute the error with each credit bureau that shows it. Also contact the business that sent the information. Explain what is wrong and why. Include copies of useful records, not your only originals. Save your dispute, proof of delivery, and any reply. The [CFPB’s dispute guide](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-dispute-an-error-on-my-credit-report-en-314/) has steps and sample letters.
If an unknown account may be identity theft, use [IdentityTheft.gov](https://www.identitytheft.gov/) for recovery steps.

sections.heading: Know what a dispute can do
paragraphs: A dispute is for information that is wrong or incomplete. It is not a way to erase correct negative information. Review the written result and check your reports again for any changes. [Read the FTC’s explanation of disputes](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/disputing-errors-your-credit-reports).
**Your next step:** Set aside time to review one report and list any items that need a closer look.

title: Credit Card Balances: Two Habits That Matter
excerpt: Paying on time and watching your balances are two different jobs. Learn how to manage both without paying interest just to build credit.

paragraphs: A credit card can feel simple until you see the statement date, due date, and several different balances. Start with two goals: pay on time and keep debt within your budget.

sections.heading: Make the due date easy to track
paragraphs: Pay at least the minimum due on time. Paying only the minimum can leave you paying interest, so pay more when your budget allows. [The FTC explains how card payments work](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/using-credit-cards-and-disputing-charges).

A phone reminder or automatic payment can help you remember. If you use automatic payments, check that your bank account has enough money and that the payment went through. Do not treat the setup screen as proof that the bill was paid. [Experian discusses payment habits and credit scores](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/how-credit-cards-can-affect-your-credit-score/).

sections.heading: Know how much of your limit you use
paragraphs: Credit utilization means the share of your available card credit that you use. For example, a reported balance of $200 on a card with a $1,000 limit is 20% utilization.

Scores can look at each card and your cards together. Lower use generally helps, but one percentage does not promise a certain score. [Read Experian’s guide to credit utilization](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/how-important-is-credit-card-utilization/).

sections.heading: Understand the balance on your report
paragraphs: Your credit report may show a balance even after you pay your bill. That is because the card company may have reported the balance before your payment. The amount on your report is not always today’s balance. [FICO explains reported balances](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/credit-scores/amount-of-debt).

sections.heading: Do not pay interest just to build credit
paragraphs: You do not need to carry debt from month to month to build a FICO score. [FICO explains this common myth](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/blog/carry-credit-card-balance-myth).

If your card has a purchase grace period and you are not carrying a balance, paying the full statement balance by the due date can avoid interest on new purchases. Check your card’s terms. Cash advances usually work differently. [See the CFPB’s grace-period guide](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-grace-period-for-a-credit-card-en-47/).
**Your next step:** Check your next due date, minimum payment, statement balance, and available bank funds.

title: Getting Your Credit Ready for a Home Loan
excerpt: Planning to buy a home? Start with your credit reports, monthly budget, and a few questions for your lender before you shop.

paragraphs: Getting ready for a home loan is about more than reaching a certain credit score. It is also about knowing what you owe and what payment fits your life. Start before you fall in love with a house.

sections.heading: Review your credit early
paragraphs: Check your credit reports for wrong accounts, balances, and payment details. If you find an error, begin the dispute process and save your records. Checking your own reports or scores does not lower your credit scores. [The CFPB explains mortgage credit checks](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-exactly-happens-when-a-mortgage-lender-checks-my-credit-en-2005/).
Do not build your home-buying plan around a promised score increase. Credit changes and loan decisions depend on your full situation.

sections.heading: Keep your money habits steady
paragraphs: Keep paying bills on time. Work on card debt within your budget. Before you apply for a car loan or a new card, consider how new debt could affect your home-loan plans. New applications can add credit checks, and new payments can change what you can afford. [The CFPB’s home-buying preparation guide](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/prepare/get-your-money-situation-in-order/) explains why this matters.

sections.heading: Set a payment you can live with
paragraphs: Look at what you actually spend, not only what you hope to spend. Review several months of bank and card statements. Leave room for costs that do not show up every month.

A lender’s preapproval amount is not your personal spending target. You can choose a lower home price that better fits your budget. Lenders consider income, assets, debts, and credit, but only you know all the needs your money must cover. [Read the CFPB’s preapproval guide](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/explore/get-a-preapproval-letter/).

sections.heading: Ask before you commit
paragraphs: Ask a lender what records are needed and what could change a preapproval. A preapproval is not a guaranteed loan. When you are ready, compare official Loan Estimates rather than choosing only by an advertised rate. [The CFPB explains what preapproval does and does not mean](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/explore/get-a-preapproval-letter/).
**Your next step:** Write down your monthly debt payments and three questions to ask a lender or a HUD-approved housing counselor.
